lesson.title: Reopening the Wound: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854
lesson.summary: Stephen Douglas's 1854 bill to organize the Kansas and Nebraska territories repealed the Missouri Compromise line and let settlers vote on slavery themselves, shattering the fragile peace built in 1850.
lesson.body:
The Kansas Nebraska Act began less as a fight over slavery than as a railroad scheme. Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois wanted a transcontinental railroad built through Chicago, which meant the vast unorganized territory west of Iowa and Missouri needed to be formally organized first. To get the bill through Congress, Douglas needed southern votes, and southern senators would not support organizing a new territory that was automatically free under the Missouri Compromise line of 1820, since the land in question sat north of the 36 degree 30 minute boundary. Douglas's solution was to apply the principle of popular sovereignty, letting the settlers of the new territories decide the slavery question for themselves by vote, the same approach used for New Mexico and Utah in the Compromise of 1850.

The bill Douglas introduced in January 1854 split the territory into two, Kansas and Nebraska, and stated explicitly that the Missouri Compromise line was superseded by the principle of popular sovereignty. In practice this repealed the thirty four year old ban on slavery north of the line, reopening a question that most Americans, North and South, had believed was permanently settled. Congress passed the bill after months of furious debate, and President Franklin Pierce signed it into law in May 1854.

The reaction in the North was immediate and severe. Many northerners who had accepted the Compromise of 1850, however reluctantly, saw the repeal of the Missouri Compromise as proof that the South would never honor any settlement and would keep pushing to expand slavery into new territory no matter what earlier deals promised. Newspapers, preachers, and politicians across the North denounced the act as a betrayal, and public anger reached a scale that the Fugitive Slave Act alone had not produced.

That anger reshaped American politics almost overnight. The Whig Party, already weakened by years of straddling the slavery question, collapsed within two years as its northern members abandoned it. Former Whigs, Free Soil Party members, and antislavery Democrats began meeting through 1854 to form a new party built explicitly around opposition to the expansion of slavery into the territories, organizing under the name Republican at gatherings including one in Ripon, Wisconsin, and a formal state convention in Jackson, Michigan, that July. Within just two years this new Republican Party would be strong enough to contest a presidential election.

On the ground, the law's popular sovereignty formula meant that whichever side could get more settlers into Kansas first would likely control the territory's future. Proslavery Missourians crossed the border in large numbers to settle and vote, while northern groups such as the New England Emigrant Aid Company organized and funded antislavery settlers to do the same. That race to control Kansas through sheer numbers, rather than through orderly political debate, set the stage for the violent conflict that would soon earn the territory its grim nickname, Bleeding Kansas.
